notes.title: Text to number checks the exponent range even when the mantissa is zero
notes.statement: Converting text to a number, measured through ABS and VALUE, rejects a zero mantissa with an out-of-range exponent: ABS("0e-309") is #VALUE! though the text denotes 0, and ABS("0e-308") is 0. notes.inferred: The exponent formula is inferred, though it fits every reading; that functions other than ABS and VALUE share this conversion is inferred.

notes.title: Subnormal cell writes and *, /, ^ underflows flush to +0, while +, - and EXP(-745) keep subnormals
notes.statement: Writing any positive or negative subnormal binary64 value or -0 to a cell via Range.Value2 stores +0 (0x0000000000000000), while normal extremes 2^-1022 (0x0010000000000000) and ±DBL_MAX (0x7fefffffffffffff) read back intact. In the 430 recorded bank rows with subnormal or maximum-finite cell arguments, all 179 subnormal-input rows read back as +0 and match the +0 control (SQRT(-5e-324) is 0, SIGN(±5e-324) is 0, ODD(±5e-324) is 1, EVEN(±5e-324) is 0, ISEVEN(±5e-324) is TRUE, ISODD(±5e-324) is FALSE, GESTEP(±5e-324) is 1, DELTA(±5e-324) is 1, and a subnormal divisor or significance in QUOTIENT, CEILING or FLOOR flushes to 0). Formula literals below 2.2250738585072014E-308 are refused at entry or parsed to 0. Products (*), quotients (/) and probed powers (^) that fall in the subnormal range flush to +0, whereas + and - retain subnormals and EXP(-745) holds 0x0000000000000001 in a formula cell. When fed a true computed subnormal x from EXP(-745), EXP(-730) or EXP(-709) (and 0-x for negative), ABS(±x) is x, SQRT(+x) is 2^-537, SQRT(-x) is #NUM!, EVEN(±x) is ±2, ODD(±x) is ±1, ISEVEN(±x) is TRUE, ISODD(±x) is FALSE, CEILING(+x,1) is 1, FLOOR(-x,1) is -1, QUOTIENT(±x,1) is 0, DELTA(x,0) is 0, DELTA(x,x) is 1, GESTEP(+x,0) is 1 and GESTEP(-x,0) is 0, while SIGN(+x) and INT(-x) transition inside the subnormal range (0 at 0x00000000001c7ea3 and ±1 at 0x0008bfe58468888d).
notes.basis: 430 bank rows replayed with Value2 input read-back and +0 controls, 22 subnormal bit-pattern cell-write probes, 16 literal-acceptance probes, 45 arithmetic underflow probes, and 180 true-subnormal function calls in Excel 16.0 build 20527 on 2026-11-08.

notes.title: AND, OR, and XOR evaluate direct arguments before references/arrays and skip direct non-boolean text unless no logical is found
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, AND, OR, and XOR inspect every argument in two passes: all direct arguments first, then references and array constants. Direct errors therefore precede errors inside arrays or references (AND({TRUE,#N/A},#DIV/0!) is #DIV/0!). Direct text "TRUE" and "FALSE" parse as logicals, whereas other direct text ("x", "1", "0", "") is skipped when at least one logical is read (AND(TRUE,"x") is TRUE, OR(FALSE,"x") is FALSE) and gives #VALUE! when none is read (AND("x"), OR("x","y")). Inside arrays and references, all text (including "TRUE") is skipped; omitted direct arguments read as FALSE in AND/OR and are ignored or FALSE in XOR (XOR(TRUE,) is TRUE).
notes.basis: Measured across all 115 Excel 16.0.20527.20088 readings in dc_fwpz (logical_functions rows 3-85) and matched across 1,210/1,210 AND, 1,212/1,212 OR, and 1,212/1,212 XOR full-bank rows.

notes.title: ASINH is LN(|x|+SQRT(x*x+1)) with every step stored, so small inputs lose their digits
notes.statement: ASINH is not the correctly rounded inverse hyperbolic sine. Its answers are those of SIGN(x)*LN(|x|+SQRT(x*x+1)), with x*x, the +1, the SQRT and the |x|+root each rounded to 64 bits and then to 53 bits before the next step, and the LN rounded to binary64. That route loses most of the digits of a small input: once x*x+1 rounds to 1, the answer is LN of |x|+1 after rounding, so it moves in steps of about 2.2E-16. ASINH(-1.4901631254755754E-16) is -2.22E-16, about 1.5 times the true value, and in the recorded rows every |x| up to 1.05E-16, including every subnormal, gives 0 on either sign. At the other end the x*x overflows: answers are finite up to the largest recorded input below it, 9.23E153, and #NUM! from the next recorded input, 2.38E154, although the true value there is about 356. In Excel build 20430 this route reproduces all 4,534 recorded rows (3,017 distinct inputs): 3,427 numbers and 1,107 #NUM!. The correctly rounded asinh matches only 1,224 of the 3,427.
notes.basis: All 4,534 rows of two recorded sets, 3,017 and 1,517 rows, from Excel build 20430. The route was recomputed independently in exact rational arithmetic with a correctly rounded LN, and matched every row. The stored steps matter on 5 of the rows (3 distinct inputs): the same formula in plain binary64 misses exactly those 5.
notes.inferred: That Excel's code is this expression, in this order, is inferred; what is measured is that the route reproduces every recorded row. The overflow boundary at |x| = 2^512, about 1.34E154, is inferred from x*x overflowing there: the recorded rows only bracket it, between 9.23E153 and 2.38E154. Excel reads a subnormal written to a cell back as 0, so the 0 at subnormal inputs may come from that step and not from this route.

notes.title: ATANH has three regimes—subnormal DAZ to +0, binary64 x + x^3/3, and signed x87 ratio-log—breaking oddness above 0x3f1af82b729c1d83
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0 build 20228 and 20430, ATANH(x) returns #NUM! for |x| >= 1, flushes both signs of any subnormal input to +0 (0x0000000000000000), evaluates ordinary binary64 x + (x*x*x)/3 for normal |x| below 0x3f1af82b729c1d83 (~1.02880227e-4), and switches at 0x3f1af82b729c1d83 to 0.5 * LN(RN53(RN64(RN53(RN64(1+x)) / RN53(RN64(1-x))))). Because the ratio branch evaluates 1+x and 1-x directly without taking |x|, ATANH(-x) != -ATANH(x) in that regime: at ±0x3f1af82b729c1d83 the positive and negative outputs differ by 4,314 ULPs (0x3f1af82b7434c926 vs 0xbf1af82b7434b84c). notes.title: BESSELI is ITK's published polynomial and recurrence, on the x87 unit
notes.statement: BESSELI truncates n to an integer and evaluates the body published in ITK with every operation stored from the x87 unit at precision 64: the I0 and I1 polynomials, and for higher orders Miller backward recurrence from j = 2*(n + int(sqrt(40*n))), rescaling by 1E-10 whenever |q| > 1E10, then normalising by I0(x). The same body in plain binary64 misses by 1 to 4 units in the last place. The published ITK body is itkGaussianOperator.hxx at ITK 311b7060ef39e371f3cd209ec135284ff5fde735 (Apache-2.0).
notes.basis: All 1,318 recorded BESSELI recorded rows match (825 gained, no row lost in the recorded rows).

notes.title: BESSELY truncates order into 0..=10,000,000 and applies a phase-shifted 2^27-1 limit that admits BESSELY(134217728, 1)
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, BESSELY(x, n) requires x > 0 and truncates n to an integer in 0..=10,000,000 (#NUM! for n < 0 such as -0.5 or n >= 10,000,001). For large x, Excel checks |x| - phase <= 2^27 - 1 using phase = 0.785398164 for Y0 and 2.356194491 for Y1 (forward recurrence orders require both seeds). Consequently, BESSELY(134217728, 1) is admitted and returns 1.1173873549496432e-05 (0x3ed7ff19f84f233c) because 134,217,728 - 2.356194491 <= 134,217,727, whereas BESSELJ(134217728, 0) returns #NUM! because 134,217,728 - 0.785398164 > 134,217,727. Subnormal operands and intermediates flush to zero.
notes.basis: Measured across all 84 BESSELY readings in DnaCalc dc96l3_bessel and 124 in dcj9k_r25_bessel (Excel 16.0.20527.20088); 2,901/2,905 full-bank BESSELY rows match.

notes.title: The beta bgrat series stops at eps, not 15*eps, and its prefactor and ratio follow the gamma-family forms
notes.statement: In the incomplete beta (TOMS 708 route) the asymptotic series bgrat is positive and truncated. DNA Calc first ran it with the published tolerance 15*eps (1.5e-14), at which its values sat on average 5.3 units low against BETA.DIST bank rows (mostly a > 15, b <= 1, x > 0.5, where Excel is unbiased); running it at eps changed BETA.DIST from 982 to 1,003 matched of 2,822 (+29, -8) and BETADIST from 140 to 142 of 294, and the mean absolute distance to Excel from 8.08 to 3.86 units, the mean signed distance from -5.31 to +0.29, rows within one unit from 1,354 to 1,432; of tolerances tried, eps gave +23 net, 2^-52 gave +22 and 1e-17 gave +21. Three Excel 20131 rows of that block (BETA.DIST(0.9375, 20.45, 0.75), (0.96875, 61, 0.2) and (0.984375, 320, 0.05), all cumulative) were 31, 33 and 13 units low at 15*eps. A later change forms bgrat's prefactor r as z times the gamma density at b, and u/r as one exponential of (n - 1/2)*LOG1P(b/a) - b*LOG1P((b-1)/(2a)) - b + s(n) - s(a) with the measured real-shape Stirling errors s: BETA.DIST went from 1,003 to 1,043 matched (+75, -35) and BETADIST by +1, and the three rows above are now 3, 5 and 3 units off. Measured and not taken: the loader beta prefactor with a fractional-shape Stirling error (in the series arm BETA.DIST +33/-51 to +31/-57 and FDIST +76/-147 to +65/-149; in the bup arm BETA.DIST +51/-65 to +70/-68, FDIST +106/-63 to +96/-63, F.DIST net -3 to -5); bgrat's gamma-tail substitution alone (+28/-27, and +81/-43 with the other two); no FDIST or F.DIST row moves in bgrat. Of the FDIST misses, 2,950 of 3,444 rows lie in the recurrence arm bup_160 and 777 of 907 in the series arm bpser; the other arms hold fewer than 10 each.
notes.basis: Three recorded Excel build 20131 BETA.DIST rows are cited with DNA Calc's distance to them before and after. The counts are quoted from the commit messages and the bead comment (full bank, per-row traces).
notes.inferred: That Excel's bgrat runs at eps and forms the prefactor and ratio through the gamma-family expressions is inferred from the match counts and the bias of the residuals; Excel's code was not read.

notes.title: Incomplete beta has no basym arm, reflects bfrac prefactors above 0.99 using caller y, and unifies bup and bgrat
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527, the incomplete-beta routine (bratio) removes TOMS 708's bratio_basym arm: all min(a0, b0) > 1.0, b0 >= 40.0 inputs stay on bratio_bfrac continuously across b = 100 and lambda = 0.03 * b (checked across 22 live bisection points). Inside bratio_bfrac, when x > 0.99 (0x3fefae147ae147ae, strict >), Excel evaluates the density prefactor as excel_brcomp(b, a, y, x) using the caller's stored complement y rather than 1.0 - x (eliminating 53-bit cancellation in F.DIST.RT, FDIST, and F.DIST), while keeping lam = |a - (a + b) * x| on x. bratio_bup runs Excel's density-based stored-power recurrence for all n >= 2 (including bup_140's n = 20 shift), using ((x * y) / a) * density with stored exp(m * ln(x)) and binary64 summation for b > 1.0, and extended-precision x^m and summation for b <= 1.0 (plus excel_log(y) in beta_density_at for a < 1 || b < 1, x > 0.99). bratio_bgrat applies the 0.99 lnx switch to all b, evaluates seeded b == 0.5 via erf/erfc, b == 1.0 via exp(-z), and z >= 1.1 via excel_gamma_fraction(b, z).
notes.basis: Measured across cb5 (1,638 live Excel 16.0.20527 calls; frozen_cb5_f_gt099_v2.jsonl 59 of 100 vs 0 of 100, 99 of 100 within 5 ULP) and nx4 (frozen_nx4_predictions.jsonl 115 of 360 vs 34 of 360). Landing nx4 moved 29 beta-family witness banks (168,767 rows) from 166,630 to 167,126 (+496 net, 0 full regressions: FDIST +206, BETA.DIST +116, BETADIST +24, CONFIDENCE.T 4,282/4,282, FINV pinned 32/32).
notes.inferred: That Excel executes these branch rules and intermediate store sites is inferred from continuity probes, frozen holdouts, and witness-bank improvements; inner-loop rounding in bfrac and non-half bgrat remain open.

notes.title: Radix converters read empty text as 0, count leading zeros toward the 10-character limit, and ignore places on negative two's-complement outputs while still validating it
notes.statement: Across the A-L Engineering radix converters in Excel 16.0 build 20430 and 20527, string inputs reject any whitespace (including spaces and tabs) with #NUM!, reject logicals with #VALUE!, count leading zeros toward the 10-character maximum (e.g. HEX2DEC("00000000001") is #NUM!), accept lowercase hex digits, and treat the empty string "" as 0 (HEX2BIN("") = "0"). When outputting a negative number in two's complement, Excel always emits 10 digits regardless of places (DEC2BIN(-512, 1) = "1000000000"), yet still requires an explicit places argument to truncate into 1..=10 (#NUM! for 0 or 11).
notes.basis: Measured across Excel 16.0.20527.20088 readings in jnt_w111_rounding and build 20430 radix batches in CalcFunc-Evidence; every listed function matches 100% of its full-bank witness rows (BIN2DEC 1,347, BIN2HEX 2,748, BIN2OCT 2,757, DEC2BIN/DEC2HEX/DEC2OCT 4,807 each, HEX2BIN 1,214, HEX2DEC 1,025, HEX2OCT 1,218).

notes.title: BINOM.INV and CRITBINOM test the public cumulative: strictly at zero successes, inclusively at later counts
notes.statement: On Excel 16.0.20527, 252 dyadic boundary designs were each asked at the exact lower tail of the binomial and at three binary64 neighbours either side. Of these, the 200 designs whose answer is a count above zero return k exactly when BINOM.DIST(k, n, p, TRUE) >= alpha, that is the smallest k whose public cumulative probability reaches alpha. The 52 designs whose answer is zero return 0 only when BINOM.DIST(0, n, p, TRUE) > alpha, so the mass at zero is compared strictly and every later cumulative inclusively. DNA Calc locates the count with a forward mass recurrence and settles it with these two public-tail comparisons; with that, BINOM.INV went from 2,290 to 2,302 of 2,308 and CRITBINOM from 1,402 to 1,414 of 1,420 full-bank rows matched, 13 won and 1 lost in each function. The lost row is (5, 0.5, 0.5).
notes.basis: The 252-design reading and its two comparison rules are quoted from the doc comment of the DnaCalc kernel, which cites Excel 16.0.20527; the two cited rows (build 20430) show the zero-count answer at alpha 0.5 for one trial and do not test the inclusive rule above zero, which no cited row locates. Counts are from the commit message and bead comment.

notes.title: BITLSHIFT and BITRSHIFT return 0 for |shift_amount| in 49..=53 and bypass the shift-count bound when number is 0
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0 build 20430, BITLSHIFT and BITRSHIFT deviate from Microsoft's published 48-bit result and 53-bit shift limits in two ways: (1) when number is 0, any finite shift_amount returns 0 (even BITLSHIFT(0, 54) = 0); (2) when number is nonzero and the truncated |shift_amount| is 49..=53, both functions return 0 instead of #NUM! (e.g. BITLSHIFT(1, 49) = 0 and BITLSHIFT(1, 53) = 0, whereas BITLSHIFT(1, 48) = #NUM! and BITLSHIFT(1, 54) = #NUM!).
notes.basis: Measured across Excel 16.0 build 20430 W111 bitwise discriminator rows in CalcFunc-Evidence cache/w111-bitwise-20260929/ and matched on 8,131/8,131 BITLSHIFT and 8,128/8,128 BITRSHIFT full-bank rows.

documentation.claim: Microsoft's BITLSHIFT and BITRSHIFT pages state that if the result exceeds 2^48 - 1 (48 bits) or |shift_amount| > 53, the functions return #NUM!, without noting that zero operands ignore finite shift_amount > 53 or that |shift_amount| in 49..=53 returns 0 instead of #NUM!.

notes.title: CELL does not trim info_type, reads the active cell when reference is omitted, and returns a two-element {width, is_default} array for "width"
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527.20088, CELL matches info_type case-insensitively without trimming whitespace (so CELL(" format ", B2) is #VALUE!). Omitting reference reads the workbook's active cell (so CELL("address") on another sheet returns the active sheet and cell such as [oracle.xlsx]Data!$A$1). CELL("width", ref) returns a 1x2 array {width, is_default} where width is the rounded column width (0 when hidden) and is_default is TRUE/FALSE; legacy formulas implicitly intersect this array to the width number. CELL("prefix", ref) emits ', ", ^, or \ only for text constants and "" for numbers, formulas, logicals, errors, and blanks.

notes.title: CHAR and CODE use the Windows-1252 code page (CHAR(128) is U+20AC, astral characters give CODE 63), while UNICHAR/UNICODE use Unicode scalar values

notes.title: COMBIN and COMBINA return 83.99999999999999 (1 ULP below 84) for C(9, 3) via cyclic x87-stored factors with * n last
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0 build 20228, COMBIN(n, k) truncates n and k (with subnormals treated as signed zero and n <= 2,147,483,646), reduces k = min(k, n - k), and evaluates product(i=2..=k, (n-k+i-1)/i) * n, storing every division and accumulator product from x87 PC64 to binary64 and multiplying n last. Because 7/2 * 8/3 * 9 divides by 3 before multiplying by 9, COMBIN(9, 3) and COMBINA(7, 3) return 83.99999999999999 (0x4054ffffffffffff) instead of exact 84 (0x4055000000000000). COMBINA truncates its two arguments independently before forming total = trunc(n) + trunc(k) - 1 and evaluates trunc(n) == 0 && trunc(k) == 0 -> 1 before checking negative k, so COMBINA(-0.25, 0.75) returns 1.
notes.basis: Measured across 20,713 COMBIN discovery rows, 1,024 cyclic held-out rows, and 35,233 COMBINA identity rows in Excel 16.0 build 20228 (CalcFunc-Evidence work/w109/G4-04-combin/ and G4-04-combina/), and matched on 25,199/25,199 COMBIN and 40,991/40,991 COMBINA full-bank rows.

correct.how: Exact integer combinatorics: C(9, 3) = 9*8*7 / 6 = 84.

notes.title: Number-to-text emits 15 significant digits via an exact Q16.64 split on [1, 65536) and x87 low-nibble scaling into Q0.64 elsewhere
notes.statement: Every worksheet consumer of general 15-significant-digit number-to-text conversion (&, CONCAT, CONCATENATE, VALUETOTEXT, ARRAYTOTEXT, FIXED, DOLLAR, TEXT, TEXTJOIN, and general cell formatting) shares one routine (first_precision). For 1.0 <= |x| < 65,536.0 (0 <= exp2 < 16), Branch 1 splits the binary64 significand directly into an integer part w (1..=65535, d digits) and an exact Q0.64 fraction f with no FPU scaling, then adds the truncated half-ulp constant floor(2^63 / 10^(15 - d)); because floor(2^63 / 10^k) < 2^63 / 10^k, exact binary ties below 65,536 never round up, and [1, 10) rounds up only past +0.07204 ulp64(v). For |x| < 1.0 or |x| >= 65,536.0, Branch 2 computes p = ceil((exp2 + 1) / 3.3219) (0 for [0.5, 1)), multiplies x by 10^-p using the low-nibble-first x87 PC64 table chain (10^+-1..15, 10^+-16..240, 10^+-256) with one 10^-1 step if scaled v >= 1.0, shifts the 64-bit significand mv into Q0.64 by a truncating right shift, and adds floor(2^63 / 10^k) (k in 15..=17). That explains why [0.5, 1) and below-2^k values require +0.372036854775808 ulp64(v) to round up, while above-2^k values exhibit a period-8 oscillation +3.37203685 + 1.25 * (mv & 7) ulp64(10v). See https://github.com/DnaCalc/DnaCalc/blob/344d70dcea3ea77cbbeee1595f96694630a9610a/docs/articles/last-bit-number-text.md.
notes.basis: Measured on 21,377 probe and W111 rows (21,377 of 21,377 matched), 29 formerly failing oracle-corpus cells (29 of 29 matched across dc_q9rb, catalogue, and fn7_format_context), and three prospective frozen proofs in nx8 on Excel 16.0.20527.20196: 600 of 600 on frozen_cb9_predictions.jsonl, 32 of 32 on the 4-binade discriminator (exp2 in {-971, -486, +484, +969}, settling ceil(frexp_k / 3.3219) 32/32 vs ceil(frexp_k * log10(2)) 0/32), and 20 of 20 on the 10^-1 sliver step. Post-study witness banks: CONCAT 3,578 of 3,578, CONCATENATE 3,133 of 3,133, FIXED 3,783 of 3,783, VALUETOTEXT 2,571 of 2,571.
notes.inferred: Whether Excel implements Branch 1 via integer bit-shifts or x87 fistp+fsub is unobservable from outputs and inferred; both give identical (w, f) for every binary64 in [1.0, 65536.0).

notes.title: On basis 1 COUPDAYS walks back from maturity by its own rule, not COUPPCD to COUPNCD
notes.statement: On basis 1 (actual/actual) COUPDAYS does not always equal COUPNCD minus COUPPCD. Its rule: start at maturity and step back by 12/frequency months. Each step keeps the day of the month and clamps it to the length of the target month, and the clamped date is the start of the next step, so passing through February lowers the day for every earlier date. Stop at the last date still after settlement, call it next. The answer is the number of actual days from one period before next up to next, and this last step keeps month ends: if next is the last day of its month, the start is the last day of its month. On the other bases the answer is 360/frequency (bases 0, 2, 4) or 365/frequency (basis 3). With this rule, all 5,584 recorded rows match (4,072 distinct inputs): 5,568 numbers and 16 #NUM!, from Excel builds 20131 and 20430. Of the 967 basis 1 rows, 81 (49 distinct inputs) differ from the day count between the dates of a schedule anchored on maturity with month ends kept. For maturity 1998-06-30 with semi-annual coupons, COUPDAYS(35748,35976,2,1) is 183, from 1997-06-30 to 1997-12-30; the anchored schedule gives 184. In one recorded case all three functions were read on the same inputs: COUPNCD(44043,2958465,2,1) less COUPPCD is 44196 - 44012 = 184, and COUPDAYS is 183.
notes.basis: All 5,584 rows of three recorded sets: 3,012 and 1,512 rows from build 20430, 1,060 from build 20131. The rule was recomputed independently from the calendar and matched all 5,566 number rows with settlement at serial 61 or later, on every basis. The other two number rows have settlement 0 and basis 0, and read 180. In a study of 42 ways to walk and measure the schedule, this was the only one to match all 965 rows with basis exactly 1.
notes.inferred: The rule reproduces every recorded row; that Excel's code works this way is inferred. For basis 1 no settlement or maturity before serial 61, where Excel's calendar differs from the Gregorian one, is in the recorded rows.

notes.title: On basis 0 COUPDAYSNC is not always COUPDAYS minus COUPDAYBS
notes.statement: On basis 0 (US 30/360), COUPDAYSNC is P - A. A is COUPDAYBS, the accrued days. P is a 30/360 count between the actual previous and next coupon dates, with day 31 and the last day of February both counted as day 30. COUPDAYS on basis 0 is always 360/frequency, but P need not be: when a coupon falls on the last day of February and maturity is not a month end, P can be 88, 89 or 92 for a quarter and 178 or 182 for a half year. So COUPDAYSNC(39923,50919,4,0), with coupons 2009-02-28 and 2009-05-29, is 39: P is 89 and A is 50, where 90 - 50 would give 40. With no coupon date before settlement in Excel's calendar, the period starts at serial 0: COUPDAYSNC(33,400,2,0) is 1, and for settlement 61, maturity 456 and annual coupons COUPDAYBS plus COUPDAYSNC is 90, not 360. This rule matches all 1,664 recorded number rows on basis 0, 733 of them chosen near February, month ends and the start of the calendar.
notes.basis: 1,664 recorded rows with a number answer on basis 0, from builds 20131, 20430 and 20527, recomputed independently from the calendar. An implementation of these rules matches all 33,504 selected readings of the six coupon functions. Fictitious 1900-02-29 is not a month end here.
notes.inferred: The split into P and A reproduces every row; that Excel's code forms these two counts is inferred. For the February cases in this note only COUPDAYSNC is recorded: their A comes from the rule, not from a COUPDAYBS reading.

notes.title: DURATION and MDURATION time the redemption at S(S(off+n)-1); a one-coupon bond is not a special case
notes.statement: DNA Calc's DURATION and MDURATION give the redemption cash flow the time t = S(S(off + n) - 1), with off the fraction (E - A) / E of the first period still to run, n the number of coupons left and S the store of the x87 running sum to binary64: the sum off + n is stored, then 1 is subtracted. The earlier form, off + (n - 1), differs from it whenever the sum crosses a binade, and on the recorded rows every DURATION and MDURATION miss with n greater than 1 had the two values different while none of the 7,908 rows where they agree was a miss. A bond with one coupon left is no longer answered as off / frequency regardless of yield: it runs the same weighted ratio, so its answer depends on the yield (8 DURATION and 7 MDURATION recorded rows). Against the full bank of recorded rows this took DURATION from 7,707 to 7,859 matched of 7,884 and MDURATION from 1,113 to 1,238 matched of 1,260, with no row lost in either function. Variants that were measured and not taken: the stored time on the redemption only (7,851 and 1,231 matched); the redemption weight and the discount exponent both changed (7,710 and 1,113); every coupon weight changed (7,781 and 1,222); every weight and exponent (7,691 and 1,111); every weight with the one-coupon change (7,788 and 1,228). After the change 25 DURATION and 22 MDURATION bank rows are still unmatched.
notes.basis: All counts are quoted from the DnaCalc commit message and its bead comment (full bank, per-row traces before and after); the recorded bank rows were not re-read for this note. The two cited rows are build 20131 readings of a one-coupon bond at two yields, whose answers differ in the last place.
notes.inferred: That Excel stores S(off + n) and then subtracts 1 is inferred from the match; the bank only shows that this form, with a general loop at one coupon left, reproduces more rows than each variant tried.

notes.title: Below 0.5, ERF is a stored (4, 5) rational from a table not yet identified
notes.statement: With RN(v) meaning v rounded to 64 bits on the x87 unit and then stored to binary64, ERF.PRECISE for |x| < 0.5 is x*N(t)/D(t) with t = RN(x*x), p = RN(x*N), y = RN(p/D), and N and D Horner sums in t in which every product and every sum is RN. N has degree 4 and D degree 5, and the coefficients read off Excel's answers, order 0 upward, are N: 0x3ff1df5e70c7956b, 0x3fc201d8627a7d2c, 0x3fa6f289d165b303, 0x3f5d93a5813e372c, 0x3f2932767df264b2; D: 0x3fefada15778ece6, 0x3fdd191aca8d2499, 0x3fb79f85ba68803e, 0x3f856de5da86af12, 0x3f4609751b5b6488, 0x3ef4f20a473a5ab0. The rational stops at 0.5 itself. It equals erf to a flat 9E-17 up to 0.5, and its error climbs at once beyond, so 0.5 is its design interval and not Cody's 0.46875. No published table has been matched: Cody's 1969 rational is refuted by its linear terms, and Cephes has the same shape with different ratios. Evidence record EV-DIST-0026, which predates this note, attributes ERF.PRECISE and ERFC.PRECISE to the a < 1 branches of the NSWC GRATIO routine and says no coefficient table exists; below 0.5 this note replaces that attribution. Because every step rounds, answers need not be correctly rounded: of the 654 recorded rows of build 20131 in [0.25, 0.5), 400 differ from the correctly rounded erf, by up to 3 units, and small arguments can be 1 unit high, as below. ERFC and ERFC.PRECISE below 0.5 are 1 less this value, and GAUSS at tiny arguments takes half of it at its stored z/sqrt(2).
notes.basis: All 618,225 recorded ERF.PRECISE rows with |x| < 0.5 match; they were only scored, never used to read the coefficients, and ERFC and ERFC.PRECISE match every recorded row in that range. Two fresh sets of 60,000 random doubles below 0.5 (Excel build 20527) match 59,996 and 59,982; the second was asked after the constants were fixed, and 17 of its 18 misses are in [0.25, 0.5). With every step stored, 223 of 38,000 rows at 19 sites stay unexplained; the other store placements leave 568 to 1,244. 2,000 consecutive doubles below 0.5 match 1,988, and 2,000 from 0.5 up match 858, chance level, which places the cut.
notes.inferred: That the legacy ERF(x) shares this body is inferred: ERF.PRECISE, ERFC and ERFC.PRECISE rows were scored in full, and for ERF itself the record holds only nine non-zero single-argument inputs below 0.5 (build 19929), all equal to the rational.

notes.title: Above 0.5, ERFC rounds x*x before the exponential, so the tail drifts by hundreds of units
notes.statement: With RN(v) meaning v rounded to 64 bits on the x87 unit and then stored to binary64, ERFC for x >= 0.5 behaves as Q = E*F with z = RN(x*x) and E = exp(-z) stored to binary64, then multiplied by a factor F that is not identified. So the rounding error of x*x reaches the answer at full size. At x = 26.543000000000003, x*x exceeds z by 4.64E-14, which at the size of this answer is about 212 units, and Excel's answer is 212 units above the correctly rounded erfc. Near x = 5.93 the same effect is 23 units. For small x, where x*x is exact or nearly so, the answer stays within a few units.
notes.basis: 220,000 Excel answers from 0.5 to 26.5 (build 20527) compared with E times the true exp(x*x)*erfc(x). With z = RN(x*x) and E stored, the residual stays within about 10 units of 2^-53 at every x. At x = 24 the exact exp(-x*x) spreads with a standard deviation of 287 units, Cody's and fdlibm's fractional splits of x*x spread the same, and plain binary64 x*x leaves outliers of up to 1,024 units.
notes.inferred: F is not a closed form: y = RN(E*RN(F)) with any offset matches 40% of answers at best. Its noise tracks about a dozen smooth curves, consistent with two polynomials of degree about 8 in x with shapes near Cephes' erfc P and Q, but that is a reading of shape only, and no table has been matched.

notes.title: F.TEST is twice the smaller tail of the larger-first ratio; swapping the arrays moves the last bit on ties
notes.statement: F.TEST returns 2 * min(P(F > f), P(F <= f)) for the variance ratio f taken larger variance first, not min(2 * P(F > f), 1). With unequal degrees of freedom the right tail of the larger-first ratio can pass 1/2 even at f = 1 (equal variances, sizes 5 and 3), where the clamped form returns 1; Excel build 20228 returns 0.888888888888889 there. DNA Calc computes both tails from the one incomplete-beta call that F.DIST.RT's staging uses, taking its own complement output rather than 1 - p: that held 13 gross full-bank rows (up to 1.8e15 units off before) and took F.TEST from 21 to 26 matched of 78 with the worst miss from 1,767,616,520,413,419 units to 11, gaining 5 and losing none; the other 8 former gross rows are now 1 to 8 units off. Not ordering the ratio larger-first (var1/var2 as given) lost 8 matched rows. Equal variances give the same value with either argument order up to the last bit: the recorded answers for the two orders of the same arrays are 0x3fec71c71c71c71e and 0x3fec71c71c71c71c. A rule that orients exact ties with var1 > var2 was measured and not taken (+4 and -3 of 78 rows, against an estimate of +6 and -3).
notes.basis: Two recorded Excel build 20228 rows (the same arrays in both argument orders) are cited; DNA Calc returns the second of them, and four further recorded rows are held in DNA Calc's unit test. Row counts are quoted from the commit messages (full bank, row-by-row trace).
notes.inferred: That Excel orients the ratio larger-first and takes both tails from one incomplete-beta call is inferred from the match counts; 'ties' here means equal sample variances, and Excel's rule for choosing the orientation on them is not identified.

notes.title: FACT rejects negative fractions before truncating while FACTDOUBLE admits [-1, 0); both multiply in reverse
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0 build 20430, FACT(n) checks n >= 0 before truncating toward zero (so FACT(-0.1) is #NUM!) and returns #NUM! for n >= 171, whereas FACTDOUBLE(n) truncates first and admits [-1, 0) as 1 (so FACTDOUBLE(-0.1) = 1 and FACTDOUBLE(-1) = 1, while FACTDOUBLE(-1.1) = #NUM!). For n >= 2, both functions multiply in descending reverse order in native binary64 (n * (n - 1) * ... * 2 for FACT, n * (n - 2) * ... for FACTDOUBLE); forward products miss large values such as FACT(170). notes.title: FLOOR rounds its quotient to 15 digits first, so the result can pass the number
notes.statement: FLOOR behaves as s times the floor of number/s, where the quotient is first rounded to 15 significant decimal digits and the final product is taken in binary64. A quotient just under an integer therefore counts as that integer, and the result can exceed the number: FLOOR(0.9999999999999999,0.1) is 1. Once the quotient has more than 15 significant digits the step moves it by more than one unit, so an exact multiple can change: FLOOR(4503599627370496,2) is 4503599627370500.
notes.basis: All 931 recorded rows with normal nonzero arguments and a number answer, Excel build 20430, recomputed for this note from the recorded inputs; the 1,335 rows of that capture also hold errors, zero and subnormal cases. On the 945 rows that include subnormal quotients, the plain route matches 857 and an exact floor 848. A separate 120 literal calls in build 20527 agree. The rule was first stated from readings of this family, so these counts are in sample.
notes.inferred: That Excel's code rounds to 15 digits this way is inferred from the fit. Whether FLOOR.MATH and FLOOR.PRECISE take the same step has not been read.

notes.title: FORECAST.ETS fits histories of four or fewer points nonseasonally and extends those under seven by regression
notes.statement: In DNA Calc's implementation of FORECAST.ETS, every prepared history of four or fewer points is fitted as a nonseasonal series, whether the seasonality argument is automatic (1), an explicit 2, or 0. For a history shorter than seven points the starting series is extended to seven points before the search: the trend is the least-squares slope of the points in order (computed in plain binary64), and the point at index j (from the history length up to 6) is y[j mod 2] + (j - j mod 2) * trend. DNA Calc computed these histories under this rule and matched Excel on 199 of the 204 recorded short-history cells; the other five differ from Excel by 1 to 3 units in the last place. One recorded Excel forecast, FORECAST.ETS(5, {2,7,-1,4}, {1,2,3,4}, 2) = 1.5926883521785709, is held as a unit test. Before this change the same histories were refused unless the slope and every product and sum were exact in binary64; on the oracle corpus the passed count went from 76,480 to 76,759 and the refused count from 956 to 672, with no previously matched row lost.
notes.basis: The row counts (199 of 204 cells, +279 passed, +5 mismatched 1 to 3 units, refused 956 to 672) are quoted from the DnaCalc commit message and the code comment; the 204 cells themselves were not re-read for this note, and the one Excel reading cited is a located capture cell (the same history asked with seasonality 0; the unit test asks it with 2 and holds the same value).
notes.inferred: That Excel's own code builds the seven-point start series by this expression is inferred from the match; the five cells that differ by 1 to 3 units show the rounding of Excel's regression is not fully reproduced. Which Excel build the 204 cells came from is not stated in the commit.

notes.title: Seasonal FORECAST.ETS centers 2p sliding moving-average initials, starts smoothing at j=0, and linearly interpolates fractional CONFINT variance
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527, seasonal AAA FORECAST.ETS builds initial state over m = min(len, 5 * p) observations (extending histories shorter than ceil(3.5 * p) by tau = sum_q regression_slope(phase_q) / (p * p) via raw-moment slopes). It computes a subtract-first 2*p sliding moving average sum = (sum - e[t - 1]) + e[t + 2*p - 1], T[t] = sum / (2*p), averages detrended e[t + p/2 - 1] - T[t] per phase to form raw[q], centers seasons[q] = raw[q] - center with pre-centered initial level = (y[0] - raw[0]) + center, and sets initial trend T_0 = regression_slope(e[j] - seasons[j % p]). The smoothing loop starts at t = -1 (level = initial.level - initial.trend) and runs from j = 0, so err[0] enters MAE, RMSE, SSE, and state updates. FORECAST.ETS.STAT types 1-3 show Excel stores 6-digit rounded binary64 smoothing constants (such as 0.001, 0.0833333, 0.166667); seasonal_general re-centers seasons and adds them via x87 PC64; and FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT linearly interpolates mse * horizon_variance at fractional horizons (from 0 on h in (0, 1)) before sqrt and x87 multiplication by z.
notes.basis: Measured across nx3's live Excel 16.0.20527 frozen holdouts (frozen_ets_pred.json 32 of 48 vs 1 of 48; frozen_confint_frac_pred.json 33 of 40 vs 16 of 40) and cb4's FORECAST.ETS.STAT measurements. On the full witness banks, FORECAST.ETS moved from 2,640 to 2,959 of 2,959 (+319, worst ULP 1,440 -> 0), FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT from 4,001 to 4,355 of 4,355 (+354, worst ULP 736 -> 0), FORECAST.ETS.STAT stayed 2,955 of 2,955, and FORECAST.ETS.SEASONALITY stayed 2,958 of 2,958.
notes.inferred: That Excel executes this exact sliding moving average, j=0 indexing, and fractional variance interpolation is inferred from matching all 12,227 bank rows and the unseen frozen holdouts.

notes.title: FV uses the linear route only at exact rate = 0, so tiny rates such as 1e-15 lose over 60% via rounded 1 + rate
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0 builds 20131 and 20430, FV(rate, nper, pmt, [pv], [type]) takes the linear form -(pv + pmt * nper) only when rate = 0 exactly. For any nonzero rate, it computes factor = POWER(RN53(RN64(1 + rate)), nper), divides (factor - 1) / rate in x87 before multiplying by timing 1 + rate * type, and flushes each cashflow product before summing. At rate = 1e-15, nper = 10, pmt = -120, pv = 1000, type = 0, rounding 1 + 1e-15 in binary64 turns (factor - 1)/rate into ~11.102 instead of 10, returning 332.2676295501767 instead of the mathematical value ~200.0000000000054.

notes.title: GAMMA.DIST's prefactor carries GAMMALN(a+1) in the exponent, with its error
notes.statement: With RN(v) meaning v rounded to 64 bits on the x87 unit and then stored to binary64, the series arm and the density of GAMMA.DIST at integer shape a from 2 to 6 share r = RN(exp(t - x - GAMMALN(a+1))), with ln x stored, t = RN(a*ln x), and the difference held in the 64-bit registers. The cumulative answer is RN(r*S) with S the stored forward sum, and the density RN(r*a)/x, the division last; with a scale, y = RN(x/beta) comes first. So GAMMALN's own error is in every answer: at shape 2 the constant is GAMMALN(3), one unit above stored ln 2 (FN-GAMMALN-001).

notes.title: Incomplete gamma at integer shape 2 to 20 is a stored polynomial of reciprocal factorials times EXP(-x)
notes.statement: For an integer shape a from 2 to 20 and a < x <= 30, DNA Calc computes the upper tail as Q(a, x) = S(EXP(-x) * H), with H a Horner polynomial whose coefficients are 1/k! rounded once to binary64 (k = 0 to 19) and with every Horner multiply and add stored to binary64 before the next step; the result is EXP(-x) times the stored polynomial, and P = 1 - Q. The boundaries were located with adjacent-double probes: a == x and x > 30 do not take this route (they take the ordinary gamma-density route), and a divided Horner form, a forward term sum, and an extension to a >= 21 were each refuted. Over the full bank this matched 20 more rows net (3,889,422 to 3,889,442): CHIDIST +6, CHISQ.TEST +1, GAMMA.DIST +5, POISSON.DIST +3, GAMMA.INV +6 and -1, with four rows lost: CHIINV (0.001, 10), CHISQ.INV (0.6, 4) and (0.85, 4), GAMMA.INV (0.75, 5, 1); the first three are exact-inverse pins whose gains in the same functions offset them. On the oracle corpus the passed count went from 76,759 to 76,765. Measured and not taken: for large-mean POISSON, one stored product M*u*A gave +79 and -73, and M = RN64(V/D) resident into st(M*u) then st(T*A) gave +47 and -39 on the 542 large-mean POISSON misses, with gains and losses interleaved inside the same (k, mean) groups so no clean rule; a stored generic GAMMA seed fixes GAMMA(-0.5) and GAMMA(-1.5) but breaks GAMMA(-2.5), which matches today.
notes.basis: Counts and boundaries are quoted from the DnaCalc commit message, code comments and bead comment (full-bank per-row traces); the two cited build 20131 rows are readings at integer shapes 2 and 3 inside the region, not a test of the polynomial's stores.
notes.inferred: That Excel evaluates this polynomial with these coefficient loads and stores is inferred from the match and from adjacent-double probes; the coefficient loads are described in the code as conditional on the other loads and on EXP.

notes.title: Forward incomplete gamma runs finite sums strictly on a < x <= 30, drops ln(10) and x0=31 splits for a <= 20, and loops forward for a > 20
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527, the shared forward incomplete-gamma kernel gratio(a, x) removes three splits of NSWC TOMS 708. First, for integer shapes a in 2..=20 and half-integer shapes a in 1.5..=19.5, the finite-sum branch runs strictly on a < x <= 30.0: at x == a Excel runs the lower Taylor series (matched on 42 of 42 adjacent-double boundary calls), and for half-integers Excel evaluates a stored x87 PC64 Horner polynomial over RN53(2^(k+1) / (2k+1)!!) scaled by exp(S(-x - S(0.5 * ln(x)))) * (1 / sqrt(pi)) * x plus ERFC.PRECISE(sqrt(x)). Second, for 1 < a <= 20 outside the finite sums, Excel has no ln(10) switch and no x0 = 31.0 asymptotic switch: x <= a runs the forward Taylor series and x > a stays in the continued fraction down toward DBL_MIN. Third, for a > 20 and x / a >= 1.3 (all x, with no x0 = 31.0 threshold), Excel computes the upper tail by a forward x87-stored loop (amn = S(amn - 1), nt = S(t * S(amn / x)), stopping at |nt| > |t| or |t|/s <= 2^-52) multiplied by S(pm * S(S(a / x) * s)) using poisson_mass(a, x) (Loader's saddle-point prefactor for a > 1 and x > 1.1). See also the DnaCalc last-bit article https://github.com/DnaCalc/DnaCalc/blob/344d70dcea3ea77cbbeee1595f96694630a9610a/docs/articles/last-bit-gamma.md.

Offline across 12 gamma/Poisson/chi witness banks (162,739 rows), landing nx6 moved total matches from 160,287 to 161,032 (+745 net: CHIDIST pinned 120 of 120, POISSON +199, POISSON.DIST +182).

notes.title: For a < 1 and x < 1.1, Excel uses TOMS 654 double-precision st200 branch bounds with shared Kahan expm1, forcing even LSBs when P < 0.5
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527, when 0 < a < 1.0 and 0 < x < 1.1 (unit scale x / beta), gratio computes z = S(a * ln(x)) with x87 PC64 operations and selects the upper-complement branch st200 using TOMS 654's double-precision (iop = 1) bounds: z >= -ln(2) (-0x1.62e42fefa39efp-1, 0xbfe62e42fefa39ef) when x <= 0.5, and S(a - x) < 0.25 when x > 0.5. Single-bit straddles at x = 0x3fd965fea53d6e3c vs 0x3fd965fea53d6e3d (a = 0.75) and x = 0.5 vs next_up(0.5) (a = 0.8125) establish both seams with zero bits of slack. Inside st200, Excel computes expm1(z) via its shared Kahan excel_expm1_internal(z) routine (not Morris's gratio_rexp rational) and forms P = 0.5 + (0.5 - qans), which by Sterbenz's lemma gives an even LSB (bit 0 = 0) on every output with P < 0.5 (85 of 85 across consecutive-x sweeps). Separately, for CHISQ.DIST(2*y, 2*a, TRUE) at a > 20 and y < 1.1, Excel exits the anomalous a > 20 lower-series branch at y == 1.1 (0x3ff199999999999a) while poisson_mass keeps compensated exp until y > 1.1.

notes.title: Gamma and chi-square inverses use erfinv(p)^2 at a=0.5, Goldstein 451 for a > 1, a 0.9999 complement switch, and damped Halley
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527, the five gamma and chi-square inverse functions share one unit solver plus closed forms. At alpha == 0.5 (df == 1), Excel computes erfinv(p)^2 directly using the exact same four-piece rational/AS 241 tables as NORM.S.INV (omitting sqrt(2) on the central pieces and scaling the AS 241 tail by 1/sqrt(2)), flushing subnormal y*y to 0.0 inside the unit helper before multiplying by beta or 2.0. For general shapes, a > 1.0 starts from Goldstein (1973, CACM Algorithm 451) 7-term stored polynomial a * ((c * c) * c) (with z = -NORM.S.INV(q) on right-tail CHIINV/CHISQ.INV.RT for df >= 3 so tiny q never collapses 1 - q to 1.0); a < 1.0 uses AS 91 -1.24 * ln(p) power-law or Wilson-Hilferty with a * exp(3 * ln(c)). Above strict prob > 0.9999 (0x3fefff2e48e8a71e), the Halley residual switches to the upper/lower complement (comp(prob) - flush(Q) or flush(P) - comp(prob)). The unfactored Halley step uses AS 109 thirding damping on sign changes, a 106-trial budget, and stops on |next - x| <= eps * x (returning best_x by strict < on |df| without evaluating next) or |last_adj| >= step_limit && !improved. Remaining >= 5 ULP misses on GAMMA.INV/GAMMAINV sit almost exclusively in a < 1, y < 1.1 where conditioning ~ 1/a magnifies forward gratio offsets. See https://github.com/DnaCalc/DnaCalc/blob/344d70dcea3ea77cbbeee1595f96694630a9610a/docs/articles/last-bit-gamma.md and https://github.com/DnaCalc/DnaCalc/blob/18828c4446e1375dd58ab855ea87c09d649b2e67/docs/articles/last-bit-normsinv.md.
notes.basis: Measured across cb6 (140 of 140 on a==0.5 / df==1 frozen holdout; 291 of 500 overall), nx6 (20 of 20 on a > 20 GAMMA.INV), and nx7 (30 of 30 on |next - x| <= eps*x, 57 of 60 on a*exp(3*ln(c)) + stop rule, 51 of 65 on damping stop). Across the 5 inverse witness banks (20,160 rows before nx9 expansions), nx5..nx7 raised exact matches from 17,712 to 19,430 (CHIINV 4,290/4,293 worst 2 ULP, CHISQ.INV 2,900/2,903 worst 2 ULP, CHISQ.INV.RT 4,190/4,191 worst 2 ULP).

notes.title: GAMMALN from 3 to 8 is a stored recurrence, and GAMMALN(3) is one unit above ln 2
notes.statement: With RN(v) meaning v rounded to 64 bits on the x87 unit and then stored to binary64, write x = n + y with n the integer part. For 3 < x < 8, Excel forms z = (y+2)(y+3)...(y+n-1) from the left with every product RN, and GAMMALN(x) is RN(RN(ln z) + GAMMALN(2+y)). So answers on this range carry the rounding of a value on [2,3]. x = 3 itself belongs to the band on [2,3], not to this route, and returns 0x3fe62e42fefa39f0, one unit above the stored ln 2, although GAMMALN(3) is exactly ln 2.

notes.title: GROUPBY and PIVOTBY hold an array returned by their LAMBDA inside its cell; INDEX boxes it unless computed, and N(boxed) is #VALUE!
notes.statement: Measured in Excel 16.0.20527 through COM (dc-h9u), when a GROUPBY or PIVOTBY callback LAMBDA returns an array, Excel keeps that array held inside its result cell rather than flattening or failing immediately: a cell spilling that held array shows #VALUE!, an operator over the result is #VALUE! in a dynamic-array formula (and takes the first element in a legacy formula), SUM/COUNT/COUNTA read across its elements, and MAX/MIN/AVERAGE/PRODUCT/SUMSQ give #N/A. INDEX(GROUPBY(...), 1, 2) returns a boxed array that displays its first element (so *10 multiplies the first element and TYPE gives 1, while SUM/ROWS/CONCAT read the whole array); however N(INDEX(GROUPBY(...), 1, 2)) returns #VALUE!, and omitting the column selector as INDEX(INDEX(GROUPBY(...), 0, 2), 1) leaves the inner array held (#VALUE!). When the group LAMBDA builds a computed array (for example LAMBDA(x, x+0), TRANSPOSE(x), or FILTER(x, x>0)), INDEX(GROUPBY(...), 1, 2) spills that array in a dynamic-array formula. In PIVOTBY with several value columns and one function, Total and column subtotal columns are blank; with several functions they carry values.
notes.basis: Read from Excel 16.0.20527 COM measurements recorded in DnaCalc commits ad40ea44 (about 160 dynamic-array and legacy grouping formulas), a61f6695 (15 PIVOTBY multi-field depth calls), d96d8cba (held_arrays explicit dynamic-formula tests), and 2,055 grouping rows in catalogue sheet dch9u_functions.

notes.title: A direct error stops these array functions; the same error in an array or cell is an element
notes.statement: An error written directly as an argument of these functions is the answer for the whole call. It is not placed in the result: HSTACK(1,#VALUE!) is #VALUE!, not a row holding 1 and an error, and TAKE(#N/A,0) is #N/A. With MAP the LAMBDA does not run at all: MAP(NA(),LAMBDA(xx,IFERROR(xx,3))) is #N/A. The same error inside an array, or in a referenced cell, is an ordinary element: MAP({#N/A},LAMBDA(xx,3)) is 3, and HSTACK(Data!C1,{1;2}) with #N/A in Data!C1 is a 2 by 2 array with #N/A in its first column. TOCOL and TOROW show the difference with ignore 2: TOCOL(#N/A,2) is #N/A, while TOCOL({#N/A},2) drops the error, has nothing left, and is #CALC!. EXPAND is an exception on the cell side: EXPAND(Data!C1,2,2,"pad") is #N/A for the whole call. BYROW and BYCOL check the direct error first too: BYROW(#N/A,#VALUE!) is #N/A, while BYROW({#N/A},2), where 2 is not a LAMBDA, is #VALUE!.
notes.basis: 27 recorded readings in dynamic-array Excel, each with size observers.

notes.title: IFS and SWITCH pass on the selected value whole, and later arrays do not lift the call
notes.statement: Once a scalar test selects a result, array arguments after it have no effect on the shape: IFS(TRUE,1,{FALSE,TRUE},{2,3}) and SWITCH(2,2,1,{1,2},3) each return one 1, not an array, and SWITCH("A","a",1,{"A","A"},2) returns 1 because the match ignores case. The selected value itself is passed on as it is. A selected reference stays a reference: ISBLANK(IFS(TRUE,Data!Z1)) is TRUE over an empty cell. A selected LAMBDA shows as #CALC! in the cell, IFS(TRUE,LAMBDA(xx,xx)), and a selected array of LAMBDAs as #CALC! in each cell. A test that is not TRUE or FALSE gives #VALUE! in the shape of its result: IFS("2",{"hit","hit"}) is {#VALUE!,#VALUE!}. A direct error as the SWITCH expression stays one error: SWITCH(#VALUE!,1,{1,2},0) is #VALUE!.
notes.basis: 11 recorded selection readings in dynamic-array Excel, each with size observers.

notes.title: IPMT and PPMT reuse PMT's quotient, one through expm1 and the other through exp
notes.statement: With RN(v) meaning v rounded to 64 bits on the x87 unit and then stored to binary64, take L and q from PMT (FN-PMT-001; with nonzero fv, q = RN(N/em) with an fv numerator that is open). For period k of nper with end-of-period payments, m = nper-k+1, t = -(m*L), em_m is the expm1 of t by the route in FN-PMT-001, and u = exp(t) stored. Then IPMT = -RN(RN(RN(q*em_m) - RN(fv*u))*rate) and PPMT = RN(RN(RN(q - fv)*u)*rate). Interest takes the Kahan expm1, and principal takes the exponential it starts from: 1+em_m fits 36 of 74 principal rows where u fits all 74. So neither answer is the payment less the other (FN-PPMT-001).
notes.basis: fv 0, type 0: IPMT 95 of 95 and PPMT 74 of 74 recorded rows, plus 64 of 64 fresh PPMT(r,1,1,pv) and PPMT(r,1,2,pv) readings. Nonzero fv, type 0: PPMT 25 of 27, IPMT 18 of 27. Over every recorded row in the evidence repository IPMT matches 48 of 57 and PPMT 26 of 33. Replaying the formulas in exact rational arithmetic, with exp and ln correctly rounded, gives all 12 PPMT and all 12 IPMT answers of the loan below.

notes.statement: Text or a logical typed directly as the values argument of IRR is not an error of type: "", "2", "x", "0", "-2", TRUE and FALSE all give #NUM!, never #VALUE!. notes.title: IRR with an exactly zero first NPV answers 1/v - 1 from the stored v = 1/(1+guess), not the guess
notes.statement: In DNA Calc's secant iteration for IRR the first point is v = 1/(1+guess), stored to binary64. When the NPV at that point is exactly zero, the answer is 1/v - 1 computed from the stored v, not the raw guess, so two guesses that store the same v give the same answer. This took IRR from 533 to 549 matched of 734 full-bank rows, 16 won and none lost. Two other details were measured against the same rows. A residual taken from the raw guess, proposed in the research answer, was refuted: it netted -3 on the bank and -10 on 200 fresh two-flow problems and missed its own target row. The 200-step iteration cap was kept because a cap of 20 lost 3 matched rows. 185 IRR bank rows were unmatched when the bead comment was written.
notes.basis: Counts are quoted from the DnaCalc commit message and the bead comment (full bank, per-row trace). The three cited rows are build 20131 readings: five guesses within 4 units in the last place of 0.21 for the same cash flows (three shown) all answer 0.20999999999999996, not the guess; they show the answer follows the stored v and are not themselves a zero-NPV test.

notes.title: LOWER leaves letters above U+FFFF alone, and a combining mark stops the final sigma
notes.statement: LOWER did not change the Deseret capital U+10400, a cased letter above U+FFFF, either alone or inside other text: LOWER("A𐐀Σ") is "a𐐀ς", where the Greek capital sigma at the end becomes the final form. Greek sigma depends on what follows: followed by a full stop it takes the final form ς, and followed by a combining mark, U+0300 or U+0301, it takes the medial form σ. PROPER treats a character above U+FFFF as a word boundary, so PROPER("a𐐀b") is "A𐐀B", with the B capitalised and the Deseret letter unchanged.
notes.basis: 6 recorded LOWER and 4 recorded PROPER readings, in a workbook at compatibility version 2.
notes.inferred: The readings cover one Deseret letter and two combining marks. That every letter above U+FFFF and every mark behave the same is inferred.

notes.title: MOD with tiny operands gives wrong signs and #NUM!, by a rule that fits every recorded row
notes.statement: MOD(n,d) takes the exact remainder r of n by d and adds d when their signs differ. Three things change when r is subnormal and its sign differs from d's. The result is #NUM! when |n/d| is 2^26 or more, or when d's low part under a Veltkamp split at 2^27 + 1 is subnormal. Otherwise, when |r| is below 2^-1026, the result is |d| + |r| with d's sign: the remainder is added where it should be taken away. A larger r takes the ordinary step. Any subnormal final result is #NUM!. So MOD(-(1+121*2^-52)*2^-983, 2^-983) returns +(1+121*2^-52)*2^-983, and MOD(2^-983, -(1+120*2^-52)*2^-983) returns #NUM!, where the exact answers are ordinary numbers.
notes.basis: All 152,432 recorded MOD rows match, 4,974 of them rows the ordinary step misses, and so do 1,128 new Excel readings (build 20527). Those readings overturned an earlier test on power-of-two divisors: 1E-296 behaves like a power of two and 1E-300 does not.
notes.inferred: The rule is what is measured. Reading it as Veltkamp's split, the parts of a Dekker product of the count and the divisor, is an interpretation: a table over exponent and trailing zeros puts the boundary between exponents -1000 and -990 and at about 27 trailing zeros.

correct.how: MOD(n,d) = n - d*INT(n/d) in exact rational arithmetic; the result is exactly representable.

notes.statement: MODE, MODE.SNGL and MODE.MULT take only numbers from their arguments, even when text or a logical is typed directly into the call. notes.title: MROUND counts a quotient within 5E-15 below a half up
notes.statement: MROUND(n,m) forms q = n/m on the x87 unit and stores it to binary64, counts floor(q), adds 1 when 0.5 - frac(q) <= 5E-15, and returns count*m from the x87 unit. A number just below a half therefore rounds up though it is nearer the lower multiple: 0.499999999999995 with multiple 1 gives 1, and the next binary64 below it gives 0. MROUND(6.05,0.1) stays 6, because its quotient 60.49999999999999 lies 7.1E-15 below the half.
notes.basis: All 50,782 recorded MROUND rows match this rule. The cut-off lies between the adjacent binary64 values 4.996E-15 (rounded up) and 5.0515E-15 (rounded down) from 0.5, measured at floor(q) = 0 over 4,264 rows.
notes.inferred: The window is measured between two neighbouring values; that the constant is the decimal 5E-15 is inferred, as the decimal in that window.

documentation.claim: MROUND rounds up, away from zero, if the remainder of dividing number by multiple is greater than or equal to half the value of multiple.

notes.title: MULTINOMIAL sums log10(2..=total), subtracts log10(2..=item) in reverse argument order, and rejects total > 170
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527, MULTINOMIAL truncates each admitted argument toward zero (negative gives #NUM!), rejects total > 170 with #NUM!, accumulates acc = sum_{k=2..=total} excel_log10(k), then loops over the flattened items in reverse order (last argument first, first argument last) subtracting excel_log10(2..=item), and finishes with POWER(10.0, acc). Because acc climbs toward log10(170!) ~ 306.8 before subtracting the item logs back down, rounding at larger exponents leaves systematic drift (up to 4,672 ULP on single-argument inputs, where acc < 0 also triggers POWER's 1.0 / p reciprocal and even LSBs) and makes MULTINOMIAL non-commutative: MULTINOMIAL(4, 108) differs from MULTINOMIAL(108, 4) by 107 ULP.

notes.title: NEGBINOMDIST evaluates Loader's saddle-point mass times p/(s+f), drifting on exact dyadic rationals at p = 0.25
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20131 and 16.0.20527, the legacy PMF-only NEGBINOMDIST(number_f, number_s, probability_s) rejects raw number_f < 0 before truncating counts toward zero, requires truncated s >= 1 and 0 < p < 1 (#NUM! otherwise), preserves subnormal exp(s * ln(p)) at f = 0, and for f > 0 evaluates the saddle-point binomial mass of s - 1 successes in s + f - 1 trials with -ln(s + f) in the running exponential followed by stored RN53(RN64(p / (s + f))) (flushed if subnormal). On exact dyadic rationals =NEGBINOMDIST(10,5,0.25) and =NEGBINOMDIST(1,5,0.25), Excel is 1 ULP low and 2 ULP high.
notes.basis: Measured across Excel 16.0.20131 (1,801/1,804 full-bank and 120/120 pinned NEGBINOMDIST rows) and 16.0.20527.20088 in dcztvv_r24 (rows 3876, 3889) and prefix_metadata (row 160).

notes.title: NETWORKDAYS.INTL checks weekend before the dates, WORKDAY.INTL after them
notes.statement: The two functions read their arguments in different orders. NETWORKDAYS.INTL decodes weekend first: with #REF! in the cell for start_date and weekend 0, the answer is #NUM!, from the invalid weekend. WORKDAY.INTL reads start_date first and gives #REF! for the same arguments. An error held in the weekend cell is also treated differently: with start 2 and second argument 5, NETWORKDAYS.INTL gives #VALUE! and WORKDAY.INTL gives #NUM!. Neither returns the error itself. A logical weekend is read as a number: NETWORKDAYS.INTL(2,5,TRUE) is 4, as with weekend 1, and FALSE is #NUM!, as with weekend 0. WORKDAY.INTL does the same.
notes.basis: 19 NETWORKDAYS.INTL and 20 WORKDAY.INTL readings with errors held in cells, and the logical weekend readings of the argument sheets.

notes.title: NORM.DIST and NORMDIST densities store x87 z, divide EXP(-z^2/2) by stdev before 1/sqrt(2*pi), and flush subnormals

notes.title: NORM.S.INV uses AS241 tails (p < 0.075 and p > 15/16) and three x87-stored rational/Padé pieces for sqrt(2)*erfinv(2p-1) in between
notes.statement: Excel's standard normal inverse (NORM.S.INV and NORMSINV) partitions (0, 1) asymmetrically: Wichura's AS241 formula runs for p < 0.075 and p > 15/16 using x87 FYL2X + FSQRT stored sqrt(-ln v), while the middle computes sqrt(2) * erfinv(t) with t = 2*(p - 0.5) across three pieces: for s = RN(t*t) <= 0.5, a degree-7/7 rational interpolant at the 15 zeros of T15 on [0, 0.73] solved near 100-bit precision; for sqrt(0.5) < |t| <= 0.85, a degree-7/5 rational interpolant times sqrt(-ln(1 - |t|)); and for 0.85 < t <= 0.875 (p in (0.925, 15/16]), a degree-9/9 Padé approximant centred at 225/256 solved at 96-bit precision times sqrt(-ln(1 - t)), storing every Horner product and sum from x87 64-bit precision to binary64. NORM.INV/NORMINV return mu + sigma*z, LOGNORM.INV/LOGINV return EXP(mu + sigma*z), and CONFIDENCE/CONFIDENCE.NORM return NORM.S.INV(1 - alpha/2)*sigma/SQRT(size) with stored steps. See https://github.com/DnaCalc/DnaCalc/blob/4fb9b728df8a96546ae685589b47e057b7e26771/docs/articles/last-bit-normsinv.md.
notes.basis: Matched across 21,898 of 21,898 full-bank witness rows across all eight functions in Excel 16.0.20527 (NORMSINV 2,210/2,210, NORM.S.INV 2,206/2,206, NORM.INV 2,915/2,915, NORMINV 2,914/2,914, LOGNORM.INV 2,911/2,911, LOGINV 2,916/2,916, CONFIDENCE 2,910/2,910, CONFIDENCE.NORM 2,916/2,916), plus 32,452 of 32,452 frozen piece-C inputs and 1,230,456 distinct sweep inputs (docs/articles/last-bit-normsinv.md).
notes.inferred: The exact polynomial solve precisions (~100 bits for piece A and 96 bits for piece C) and compiled code structure are inferred from output-bit discriminators (such as p = 0x3fed999bc5f0efd8) and frozen holdout runs rather than source inspection.

notes.title: NUMBERVALUE falls back to the host VALUE grammar for letter/digit separators and rounds 15-digit mantissas by reciprocal
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527 (en-ZA), when given a separator outside ".", ",", " ", or U+00A0 on text its own reader refuses, NUMBERVALUE strips group_separator before the first decimal_separator, replaces decimal_separator with the host decimal separator, and parses via the host VALUE grammar (e.g. NUMBERVALUE("%1e3", ".", "e") is 0.13, while NUMBERVALUE("1e-3", "e", ",") is #VALUE!). On 15-digit mantissas such as "600757912143053e-27", Excel divides by 10^27 rather than correctly rounding to binary64, differing by 1 ULP on 48 of 366 fn12 pinned rows. In compatibility-version-1 workbooks, @NUMBERVALUE evaluates to #NAME?.

notes.title: Punctuation before a Japanese repeat mark sorts one way after a Latin letter, the other after Han
notes.statement: Comparing a string with punctuation before a repeat or prolonged-sound mark against the same string without the punctuation, the order depends on the character at the start. After a Latin letter the punctuated string is smaller: "a-ゝx" < "aゝx". After a Han character it is larger: "時-ゝx" > "時ゝx". This held for every pair read, with the marks ゝ, 々 and ー and with hyphen-minus, U+2212 and U+2019 as the punctuation. In all 66 readings the two strings are never equal, and a string with the mark added sorts after the string without it, after Latin and after Han alike: "a−ゝ" > "a−".
notes.basis: 66 recorded readings of =, < and > on 22 pairs of strings, 11 pairs after 時 and 11 after a.

notes.title: PMT takes ln(1+rate) from a series, and stores its quotient before the rate
notes.statement: With RN(v) meaning v rounded to 64 bits on the x87 unit and then stored to binary64, PMT with fv 0 and type 0 at rates from -1/3 to 1/2 runs: s = rate/(2+rate); L = 2s + 2s*(s^2*T), where T = 1/3 + s^2/5 + ... + s^20/23 by Horner, all in plain binary64, which is the atanh series for ln(1+rate) (Abramowitz and Stegun 4.1.27) with the 2s term added last; t = -(nper*L); u = exp(t) stored; em = RN(RN(RN(u-1)*t)/ln(u)) for |t| < 1, and RN(u-1) otherwise, Kahan's way of forming expm1; q = RN(pv/em); PMT = RN(q*rate). L is not the correctly rounded logarithm: at rate 0.05/12 it is 0x3f7107fd59addc8a, one unit below 0x3f7107fd59addc8b, and the common 30-year loan below comes out 1 unit from the correctly rounded payment.
notes.basis: For each of 1,184 rates one binary64 L reproduces Excel's em at every nper (1,622 of 1,622 power-of-two and 1,849 of 1,849 other nper, L taken from nper 1 alone). The series gives that L at 1,181 rates; the correctly rounded log1p and fdlibm's log1p each give it at 667. Order and precision of the last two steps: in all 4,802 groups of recorded answers sharing (rate, nper) with 8 or more pv values, these steps admit one em; a binary64 quotient leaves 59 groups with none, and binary64 for both steps 111. 720 of 720 fresh type 0 rows over 20 rates, both signs, match (Excel build 20527). Over every recorded PMT row, types and fv included, 279,887 of 291,978 match.
notes.inferred: The range -1/3 to 1/2 is where twelve series terms converge, not a measured Excel boundary. Rate 0.419, near sqrt(2)-1, misses by 1 unit, so a range reduction may start there. Negative rates rest on 20 rates' controls and the recorded rows.

notes.title: Upper-tail incomplete gamma for a <= 20 runs uncontracted Modified Lentz with TINY=1e-30, and poisson_mass switches at <= 1.1
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527, all upper-tail incomplete-gamma calls with a <= 20.0 (both a < 1.0, x >= 1.1 and 1.0 < a <= 20.0, x > a outside finite sums) evaluate the uncontracted Legendre continued fraction using Thompson-Barnett Modified Lentz from b_0 = 0 (f = c = TINY, d = 0.0) with Numerical Recipes TINY = 1.0e-30 (0x39b08b2a2c280291), storing each arithmetic operation to binary64 at x87 PC64, stopping at k > 0 && del == 1.0, and multiplying S(pm * f) directly without factoring a out of the fraction. At k = 0, c_0 = S(x + S(a / TINY)) rounds a * 10^30 + x into binary64, so changing TINY to 1e-50 or 1e-100 breaks about half of 10,000 tested rows. In poisson_mass(a, x), Excel switches between the compensated exponential and Loader's saddle-point expansion inclusively at x <= 1.1 || a <= 1.1 (0x3ff199999999999a, verified by single-bit bisection at 1.1 vs next_up(1.1)). POISSON(x, mean, cum) and POISSON.DIST(x, mean, cum) match across all 278 paired probes, and POISSON.DIST(k, m, TRUE) equals CHIDIST(2*m, 2*(k+1)) and CHISQ.DIST.RT(2*m, 2*(k+1)). See https://github.com/DnaCalc/DnaCalc/blob/344d70dcea3ea77cbbeee1595f96694630a9610a/docs/articles/last-bit-gamma.md.
notes.basis: Measured across cb8's 1,325 live Excel 16.0.20527 calls and frozen_cb8_predictions.jsonl (560 of 560 unseen forward calls across 6 functions matched with 0 ULP max error; 599 of 640 overall), plus nx7's frozen_nx7_proof2_pred.jsonl (50 of 50 on the 1.1 inclusive boundary). On full witness banks after nx7, POISSON reached 1,556 of 1,560, POISSON.DIST 49,707 of 49,710 decoded (0 cumulative CF/asymp/Temme misses), CHIDIST 3,241 of 3,241, and CHISQ.DIST.RT 2,858 of 2,859.
notes.inferred: That Excel executes this exact Modified Lentz recurrence and TINY constant is inferred from matching 10,000 of 10,000 offline controls, targeted del==1.0 vs nf==f tie-breakers (2 of 2), and 560 of 560 prospective forward holdouts.

notes.title: In REGEXTEST, \w takes combining marks, dot refuses CR, and case folding reaches into ranges
notes.statement: Some regular expression details in REGEXTEST differ from a plain reading. \w matches a combining mark (U+0301) and connector punctuation (U+203F), so it is not limited to letters, digits and underscore. Dot does not match CR as well as LF: REGEXTEST("a"&CHAR(13)&"b","a.b") is FALSE. \d does not match a Han character. With case_sensitivity 1, folding applies inside a character class range: É matches [é-é] and Σ matches [α-ω]. It also covers the non-ASCII partners of ASCII letters: the Kelvin sign U+212A matches k and long s U+017F matches s. ß matches its capital U+1E9E, and a Deseret letter above U+FFFF matches its other case.
notes.basis: 12 recorded REGEXTEST readings, in a workbook at compatibility version 2.
notes.inferred: The readings cover the characters named here. That \w follows the Unicode Mn and Pc categories in general, and that ranges fold by simple case folding in general, is inferred.

notes.title: ROUND counts digits in 32 bits, and the count wraps
notes.statement: ROUND cuts num_digits toward zero to a 32-bit integer D, limited to +/-2147483647, and keeps k = D + e + 1 significant digits, where e is the decimal exponent of |number| and the sum is computed in 32 bits. k of 15 or more keeps the 15-digit reading of the number; k below 0 gives 0. A large positive num_digits therefore wraps to no digits at all: for a number near 1.1E14, 2147483617 returns the number and 2147483635 returns 0. The boundaries move by exactly -e on both the +2^31 and -2^31 sides, for e from -308 to 308. num_digits of 2^31 or more acts as +2147483647 and -2^31 or less as -2147483647.
notes.basis: Under the family rules the recorded rows match ROUND 36,821 of 36,945, ROUNDUP 52,022 of 52,841, ROUNDDOWN 59,182 of 59,995 and TRUNC 50,504 of 51,317, with no row lost and each remaining failure classified in the write-up. The wrap boundary was read at every decimal exponent in the recorded rows.

correct.how: -112500000000000 is an integer, so rounding it to any non-negative number of places returns it.

notes.title: The rounding functions read 15 digits first, so ROUNDDOWN can round up
notes.statement: Before choosing a digit these functions read the number to 15 significant digits on the x87 unit: with e the decimal exponent and n = 14 - e, y = RN64(|x| * 10^n), or RN64(|x| / 10^-n) when n is negative, while 10^|n| is exact in 64 bits (|n| <= 27). A half in y goes up for ROUNDDOWN, ROUNDUP and TRUNC and down for ROUND. So digits beyond the 15th are lost even when the requested precision keeps them: ROUND(-1594628480062905,14) loses its last digit, and ROUNDDOWN(283025097725723.5,0) returns 283025097725724, larger than its input.

notes.title: Near DBL_MAX, ROUND returns NaN bit patterns that Excel treats as numbers
notes.statement: ROUND of a number near 1.8E308 can return a binary64 with an all-ones exponent field. A decimal result of 2^1024 or more keeps its 53-bit significand, and its exponent is carried into the exponent field without a check, so the bits are a NaN. ROUND, ROUNDDOWN and TRUNC return those bits; ROUNDUP gives #NUM!. The recorded rows hold 430 such ROUND rows, 102 ROUNDDOWN and 95 TRUNC, and all 627 follow this. Even ROUND(DBL_MAX,0), whose answer is DBL_MAX, returns 0x7ff000000000000a. The cell shows 2E+308 or 1.8E+308, and a pattern with its sign bit set shows 2E+308 too, with no minus. ISNUMBER gives TRUE, ISERROR FALSE, TYPE 1, ERROR.TYPE #N/A; A1=A1 and A1>0 are TRUE. =A1, N(A1), MAX(A1), ABS(A1) and IFERROR(A1,...) pass the pattern on, as does =-A1 with its sign unchanged. Arithmetic on it (A1+0, A1*1, A1-A1, SUM, ROUND) gives #NUM!, and TEXT(A1,"0") gives #VALUE!. Saved to .xlsx, each such cell is written as the error #NUM!; reopened, the cells read #NUM! until a full recalculation brings the patterns back.
notes.basis: One Excel workbook read cell by cell through Value2 on 2026-11-04, saved, reopened and recalculated; rows from the rounding write-up, 627 of 627.
notes.inferred: That one decimal-to-binary conversion routine is the source of all these patterns is inferred from the exponent-overflow encoding.

notes.title: ROUND takes ties away from zero on the 15-digit reading, so 1.005 rounds up
notes.statement: A tie in ROUND goes away from zero, not to even: ROUND(2.5,0) is 3 and ROUND(-2.5,0) is -3. The tie is judged on the 15-digit reading of FN-ROUND-002, not on the stored value. So 1.005 and 2.675, whose binary64 values lie just below the decimal tie, count as ties: ROUND(1.005,2) is 1.01 and ROUND(2.675,2) is 2.68, where rounding the stored value would give 1 and 2.67.
notes.basis: The readings below, typed as literals, and the family rule of FN-ROUND-002 over the recorded ROUND rows.
notes.inferred: That every tie follows this is inferred from the rule's fit to the recorded rows; the literal ties read directly are the ones below.

notes.title: ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN and TRUNC read num_digits from its low 16 bits
notes.statement: ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN and TRUNC take the digit count from the low 16 bits of the integer part of |num_digits|, with the sign of num_digits. If |num_digits| is 2^32 or more, or those low bits are 32768 or more, the truncation happens at 100 places (10^-100, or 10^100 for a negative count). So 65536 acts as 0, 65537 as 1, 32768 to 65535 as 100, and -2147483748, whose low 16 bits are 100, as -100. In the out-of-range case ROUNDUP adds no unit for a positive count, and gives #NUM! for a negative count when a digit is dropped.
notes.basis: Under the family rules the recorded rows match ROUND 36,821 of 36,945, ROUNDUP 52,022 of 52,841, ROUNDDOWN 59,182 of 59,995 and TRUNC 50,504 of 51,317, with no row lost and each remaining failure classified in the write-up. All 13,914 informative ROUNDDOWN and TRUNC rows with large num_digits follow the rule.

correct.how: The exact decimal expansion of this binary64 number has fewer than 32768 places, so a truncation at num_digits places returns the number itself.

notes.title: ROUNDUP adds its unit in binary64, one bit from the decimal answer
notes.statement: ROUNDUP forms the ROUNDDOWN result, converts it to binary64, converts one unit 10^-p to binary64, and adds the two on the x87 unit, storing the sum to binary64. The sum need not be the binary64 value nearest the decimal answer, so ROUNDUP(-1.125,2) is -1.1300000000000001 and ROUNDUP(3.535,2) is 3.5399999999999996. The difference shows when the result is compared with a typed 3.54.

notes.title: At tiny magnitudes ROUNDUP may add no unit, and the two signs differ
notes.statement: ROUNDUP adds no unit when the unit itself is below the normal range, whichever the sign. For a positive number it also adds none when the 15-digit reading, as binary64, lies less than 2^-1026 above the truncation; negative numbers have no such distance. So ROUNDUP(1.0001086461844975E-307,307) is 1E-307 and ROUNDUP(-1.0001086461844975E-307,307) is -2E-307, with the same digits dropped. At -1.2225E-307 and 308 places the unit, 1E-308, is subnormal, and the answer stays at -1.2E-307.
notes.basis: ROUNDUP rows match under these rules as counted in FN-ROUND-001. In the 1,148 recorded rows nearest the 2^-1026 boundary this quantity has 1 violation, itself an artefact of how the row was classified; the exact value, the reading and x minus the truncation give 54 to 547. The opposite-sign pair is a reading from Excel build 20527.

correct.how: The number has a nonzero digit past 307 places, so rounding away from zero at 307 places gives 2E-307; nearest binary64.

notes.title: SEQUENCE truncates dimensions, advances by stored additions, and puts #NUM! only in overflowing cells
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527, SEQUENCE(rows, [columns], [start], [step]) coerces its arguments in formula order, truncates positive fractional dimensions (requiring rows*columns >= 1, else #CALC!; negative or invalid dimensions give #VALUE!), and advances each cell in row-major order by one stored binary64 addition cur = cur + step rather than start + k*step. notes.statement: The worksheet SQRT is RN53(RN64(sqrt(x))): the root is rounded to the x87 unit's 64-bit significand and then stored to binary64. notes.title: SUM, AVERAGE, and AVERAGEA apply Excel's 50-exponent cancellation snap once at the final numeric addition
notes.statement: In Excel 16.0.20527 (dc-ss3b), SUM snaps its final result to +0 when the last left partial sum's binary exponent exceeds the sum's binary exponent by at least 50 (so SUM(0.1,0.2,-0.3) returns +0 rather than 2^-54). A trailing numeric 0 counts as the final addition and suppresses the snap (SUM(0.1,0.2,-0.3,0) returns 2^-54, 0x3c90000000000000), whereas trailing cell text, logicals, and blanks are skipped and do not suppress it. AVERAGE and AVERAGEA apply the same rule to their numerator before dividing by the count; SUMPRODUCT does not snap.
notes.basis: Measured across 98+ Excel 16.0.20527 probes in dc-ss3b (docs/research/sum-cancellation-2026-11-12.md) covering scales 2^-900 to 2^900, exponent gaps 49 vs 50, zero vs skipped tails, and AVERAGE/AVERAGEA/SUMPRODUCT controls; full-bank SUM (1,211/1,211), AVERAGE (1,222/1,222), and AVERAGEA (1,212/1,212) remain matched.

notes.title: For bills longer than 182 days TBILLEQ is a quadratic, not the documented formula
notes.statement: When DSM is above 182, TBILLEQ does not use the documented formula. It uses the bond-equivalent quadratic (-t + sqrt(t^2 - (2t-1)(1 - 1/p))) / (t - 1/2), with t = DSM/365 and p = price/100. At DSM 366, a bill across a 29 February, t is 1 and not 366/365. The square root is taken in extended precision and stored, RN53(RN64(sqrt)); the rest is binary64. For the row below, DSM 203, the documented formula gives 0.244038 and Excel 0.241103. Excel's bits are 22 units below the correctly rounded quadratic because of that staging.

notes.title: In TEXT, an @ applied to a number gives the General display, not the full number
notes.statement: A format of @ or @! on a number gives what General gives, not the digits of the number. TEXT(123456789012345,"@") is 1.23457E+14 and TEXT(1234567890.5,"@") is 1234567891. notes.title: TINV for p up to 0.85 is SQRT(v*(1/z - 1)) on a binary64 beta coordinate z, so its last digits follow z
notes.statement: For df >= 2 and p <= 0.85, the recorded TINV answers lie in the image of the map t = SQRT(v * (1/z - 1)) over binary64 values z, with v the degrees of freedom and z the inverse of the regularized beta at (v/2, 1/2). Because z is a double, the t found this way can sit many units from the true root of the t distribution: TINV(0.85, 25) is 176 units in the last place from the root's t only through this map. DNA Calc takes, of the two adjacent doubles that bracket the beta root, the one whose forward value is nearer p. On the full bank this took TINV from 15 to 22 matched of 32 rows (+8 and -1: TINV(0.003, 25) was lost) and its worst miss from 173 to 17 units; the oracle corpus passed count went from 76,765 to 76,769 (CONFIDENCE.T, T.INV.2T and TINV rows fixed). For p near 1 Excel uses another route: at p = 0.97 three rows are still 10 to 17 units off the t-space bisection DNA Calc keeps there.
notes.basis: Two Excel build 20131 TINV rows are cited. The mechanism and the counts are quoted from the DnaCalc commit message and bead comment (harvest 10, R3); the 32-row bank was not re-read here.
notes.inferred: That Excel computes t through z is inferred from the recorded rows lying in the image of the map; that z is the nearer-to-p bracketing double is DNA Calc's rule, with 2 of the rows in that image still off because DNA Calc's beta forward value is not Excel's.

notes.title: TRIMRANGE accepts 3 arguments (0 none, 1 leading, 2 trailing, 3 both default), rejects fractional modes with #VALUE!, and returns #REF! on an all-blank input
notes.statement: Measured in Excel 16.0.20527 on 26 catalogue calls (sheet dch9u_functions), TRIMRANGE(range, [trim_rows], [trim_cols]) takes at most three arguments and defaults both trim_rows and trim_cols to 3 (both margins). notes.title: The variance family uses raw moments with stored steps, and two tests switch it to a centered sum
notes.statement: With RN(v) meaning v rounded to 64 bits on the x87 unit and then stored to binary64, S the running RN sum of the n values and Q the running RN sum of RN(x*x), the sample variance is RN(RN(Q - RN(RN(S*S)/n))/(n-1)) and the population variance RN(RN(RN(n*Q) - RN(S*S))/RN(n*n)). Excel then uses a centered sum instead, adding RN(d*d) with d = RN(x - mean) and dividing by n-1 or n, when either of two stored tests holds: RN(RN(RN(S*S)/n)/Q) > 0.99, or RN(variance*1000) <= |RN(S/n)|. The STDEV functions are the root of this, rounded to 64 bits and then stored. So the answer depends on which path a call takes: the first two VAR.S calls below differ by a few input steps in two arguments, the first passes the 0.99 test and is correctly rounded, and the second takes the raw moments and lands 76 units high. The next pair shows the size test: scaling the inputs by 4 leaves the first path.
notes.basis: All 14,679 recorded rows of the twelve functions match: VAR.S, VAR.P, VAR, VARP, VARA, VARPA, STDEV.S, STDEV.P, STDEV, STDEVP, STDEVA and STDEVPA. Six of those rows separate the stored steps from plain binary64. 910 fresh scalar variance readings (Excel build 20527) replay exactly in rational arithmetic. Four cancellation edges were bisected to adjacent inputs; sixteen triples chosen to separate the stored ratio from 0.99*Q and from a division by 0.99 all agree with the ratio, where 0.99*Q misses all 16 and the division 14. Seven of eight magnitude brackets reach adjacent inputs, and sixteen chosen roots all need the 64-bit root followed by a store.

notes.title: On basis 1 the fictitious 1900-02-29 is not a leap day, and YEARFRAC takes serial 0 as a date
notes.statement: Excel's calendar holds a 29 February 1900, serial 60, that never existed. On basis 1 (actual/actual) it does not make 1900 a leap year: YEARFRAC(59,60,1) is 1/365, where the real 1904-02-29 gives YEARFRAC(1520,1521,1) = 1/366. Serial 0 is accepted as a date: YEARFRAC(0,5,0) is 5/360 and YEARFRAC(0,60,1) is 60/365. Reversed dates give the same answer as in order. ACCRINTM, DISC, INTRATE, PRICEDISC and RECEIVED take the same 365 and 366 on those dates: DISC(59,60,99,100,1) is about 3.65 and DISC(1520,1521,99,100,1) about 3.66.

notes.title: YIELD near par on a coupon date returns a closed-form seed with stored partial sums, not the solved root
notes.statement: On a coupon date, with redemption 100 and more than one coupon period left, YIELD at a price close to 100 does not return the root of the price equation. It returns the closed-form seed y = f * ((n*cp - d) / (d*(n+1)/2 + n*R)), with n the periods left, cp = 100*rate/f the coupon per period, R the redemption and d = price - R, whenever the Newton step (P(y) - price) / P'(y) taken at the seed is below 1e-10; otherwise the solver runs. On the recorded 20228 and 20527 rows Excel's switch lies between steps of 8.8e-11 and 1.17e-10. The association of the seed matters: DNA Calc forms the total coupon as S(S(S(n*rate)*100)/f) and the denominator as S(S(n*R + S(S(d*n)/2)) + S(d/2)), each partial result stored to binary64 before the next, and with that association 31 more full-bank rows matched (YIELD 66 to 97 of 533, none lost). The same seed is taken at a price of exactly 100: Excel does not return the coupon rate directly there, so DNA Calc's former shortcut for price 100 and redemption 100 was removed. Before the seed was introduced (commit d44aaf0a) YIELD matched 16 of 533 bank rows with a worst miss of 4.4e15 units in the last place; with the plain binary64 seed it matched 66 with a worst miss of 2,844 units. Offline, that plain binary64 order reproduced Excel's bits on 64 of the 97 small-step rows with redemption 100, against at most 58 for the x87-extended orders tried.
notes.basis: Three recorded rows are cited (Excel build 20228, near-seed discovery set); the unit test in DnaCalc holds five rows (three from 20228 and two price 100 + 1 ulp rows at a zero coupon from build 20527) and DNA Calc returns Excel's recorded bits on all five. The matched counts are quoted from the commit messages (full bank, per-row traces).
notes.inferred: That Excel's code forms this seed, with this association and this 1e-10 switch, is inferred; the seed form is read off the bank, and the switch only brackets between 8.8e-11 and 1.17e-10.

notes.title: Multi-period YIELD starts from a schedule-free par-100 seed, steps analytic Newton on 1+y/f, and publishes pre-step y when |step| <= 1e-10
notes.statement: Superseding the near-par special case in FN-YIELD-001, Excel 16.0.20527 runs one universal solver for all multi-period YIELD calls (n > 1), regardless of coupon date or redemption. It first computes a schedule-free years-to-maturity T (using US/European 30/360 / 360 for bases 0 and 4, and k + (m - s_k) / year_days for bases 1..3 where s_k uses DATE(sy + k, sm, sd) day rollover), forms d = price - 100.0 (hardcoded 100.0, never redemption), and sets the initial iterate y_0 = f * ((tau * rate * 100 / f - d) / ((tau * 100 + d * tau / 2) + d * f / 4)). Each Newton step evaluates base = 1.0 + y / f (whose rounding into [1, 2) produces +109-ULP sawtooth jumps as y crosses base binade boundaries), sums coupon and redemption terms using excel_bond_pow, and checks |step| <= 1e-10 (0x3ddb7cdfd9d7bdbb): when satisfied, Excel returns the un-updated iterate y before subtracting step (leaving up to 2,844 ULP differences when |step_0| <= 1e-10). After 100 iterations without stopping, Excel returns y_100.
notes.basis: Measured across 3,198 cb4 live Excel 16.0.20527 calls and two prospective frozen holdout suites (frozen_yield_cb4.jsonl 413 of 500, and frozen_yield_v2_cb4.jsonl 244 of 250 including 100 of 100 on bases 1 and 3 with s_k rollover). Landing nx3 moved the YIELD full witness bank from 3,053 to 3,489 of 3,489 (+436, worst ULP 2,844 -> 0) and the pinned bank from 21 to 120 of 120 (+99).
notes.inferred: The exact Newton loop form and 100-iteration fallback are inferred from matching all 3,489 full-bank rows, 120 pinned rows, and 64 of 64 consecutive-price sawtooth sweeps.
